tldr:
**Built-in tools first.** The docs say they cover most coding tasks:

- **Grep:** text *inside* files (callers, error messages, imports).
- **Glob:** files by *name or path* (`**/*.test.tsx`).
- **Edit:** a small change anchored on text that appears **once**.
- **Read + Write:** when Edit can't anchor.

**Explore incrementally.** Grep for the entry point, then Read along the imports. **Through a wrapper**, list the exported names, then search for each.

**Extensions** are for needs built-ins don't meet:

- **CLAUDE.md:** always-on rules.
- **Skill:** on-demand workflows.
- **Hook:** rules that must hold every time.
- **MCP:** external systems.
- **Subagent:** noisy work in isolation.
mentalModel: Grep is a search inside the pages; Glob reads the spines on the shelf. Edit is a precise sticker — it needs one exact spot. If the spot appears twice, rewrite the page (Read + Write). Don't read the whole library to answer one question: find the index entry and follow the references.
whatItIs:
The exam guide covers choosing and applying built-in tools (Guide §6 · TS 2.5, pp.11–12). It also covers choosing skills vs
CLAUDE.md (TS 3.2 · Skill 5, p.13) and MCP tools vs built-ins (TS 2.4 · Skill 3, p.11). The docs' tools reference and
*Extend Claude Code* page give the exact behaviour and context costs.

**Sub-concepts — each with its picture to remember**

| # | Sub-concept | 🧭 Mental model | ⭐ Exam reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Grep | A search inside the pages — finds where text is used. | ⭐ TS 2.5 · Knowledge 1, Skill 1 |
| 2 | Glob | Reading the book spines — finds files by name or path. | ⭐ TS 2.5 · Knowledge 2, Skill 2 |
| 3 | Edit | A precise sticker on one exact spot; if the spot appears twice, it won't stick. | ⭐ TS 2.5 · Knowledge 3 |
| 4 | Read + Write fallback | When the sticker won't stick, rewrite the page. | ⭐ TS 2.5 · Knowledge 4, Skill 3 |
| 5 | Incremental exploration | Find the index entry, follow the references — don't read the library. | ⭐ TS 2.5 · Skill 4 |
| 6 | Wrapper modules | A shop sign can rename the product; search for the name on the sign. | ⭐ TS 2.5 · Skill 5 |
| 7 | Skill vs CLAUDE.md | A manual on the shelf (fetched when needed) vs the rules on the wall (always seen). | ⭐ TS 3.2 · Skill 5 |
| 8 | MCP tool vs built-in | A specialist tool only gets used if its label says why it beats the familiar one. | ⭐ TS 2.4 · Skill 3 |
| 9 | Grep/Glob absent by default on macOS/Linux/WSL | Same two questions, asked through Bash (`grep`, `find`). | 📘 docs only |

**Grid 1 — which built-in tool?** (docs + guide)

| # | Question | Tool | Not this | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Where is `process_refund(` called? | ⭐ **Grep** | Glob | The answer is text inside files |
| 2 | Which files are `*.test.tsx`? | ⭐ **Glob** | Grep | The answer is a naming pattern |
| 3 | Change one line whose text is unique | ⭐ **Edit** | Write | Targeted, small, safe |
| 4 | Change one of two identical lines | ⭐ **Read + Write** (or a longer unique anchor) | Edit with `replace_all` | Edit needs exactly one match |
| 5 | Understand how a refund is approved | ⭐ **Grep** entry point → **Read** along imports | Read everything | Context goes on what matters |
| 6 | Who calls a wrapper's functions? | ⭐ **Read** the exports → **Grep** each name | Grep the original names | Re-exports can rename them |

**Grid 2 — built-in vs extension surface** (docs: *Extend Claude Code*)

| # | Surface | What it's for | Loads | Context cost | Enforced? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Built-in tools | Files, search, shell, web — most coding tasks | Always there | Tool definitions | — |
| 2 | CLAUDE.md | ⭐ Always-on conventions (“use pnpm”) | Every session, full content | Every request | No — an instruction |
| 3 | Skill | ⭐ On-demand workflows and reference (`/deploy`) | Description each session; content when used | Low until used | No — an instruction |
| 4 | Hook | Rules that must hold every time; automation on events | On its event, outside the conversation | Zero unless it returns output | **Yes** |
| 5 | MCP server | ⭐ External systems' tools and data | Tool names at start; schemas on demand | Low until used | — |
| 6 | Subagent | Noisy work in isolation; only a summary returns | When spawned | Isolated | — |
howItWorks:
1. **Name the question.** Text inside files → Grep. Files by name → Glob. A change → Edit.
2. **Edit needs one exact match.** If the text appears twice, give a longer unique anchor, or Read the file and Write it back.
   Use `replace_all` only when **every** match should change.
3. **Explore from an entry point:** Grep for it, Read it, follow its imports. Stop when the question is answered.
4. **Through a wrapper:** read what it exports (it may rename things), then Grep for each exported name.
5. **When built-ins aren't enough**, pick the extension by the need. Always-on rule → CLAUDE.md. Occasional workflow →
   skill. Must-hold rule → hook. External system → MCP. Noisy side task → subagent.

grounding.text: Grep searches file contents for a pattern (ripgrep regex syntax; respects .gitignore); output modes: files, content lines, counts.
Glob finds files by path pattern; ** matches any depth (e.g. **/*.js); results sorted by modification time, capped at 100.

Read returns a file's contents with line numbers; Write creates or overwrites a file; Edit replaces an exact old_string that must appear exactly once — otherwise give more surrounding context or set replace_all: true. Claude reads a file in the conversation before editing it.
On macOS, Linux and WSL the Grep and Glob tools are absent by default; Claude searches with grep and find through Bash instead.
Built-in tools cover most coding tasks; the extension layer adds CLAUDE.md (always loaded), skills (on demand), MCP (external services), subagents (isolated context) and hooks (run on events).

CLAUDE.md loads every session; a skill's description loads each session and its full content when used; MCP tool names load at start with schemas deferred; subagents get isolated context; hooks cost no context unless they return output.
An instruction such as 'never edit .env' in CLAUDE.md or a skill is a request, not a guarantee; if a rule must hold every time, make it a hook.
MCP connects Claude to external services (tools and data); skills carry knowledge and workflows, including how to use those tools well.
Grep for content search; Glob for path patterns; Read/Write for whole files and Edit for targeted changes by unique text; Read + Write when Edit can't find a unique anchor.

Skills: Grep to find callers or error messages; Glob for naming patterns like **/*.test.tsx; Read then Write when Edit can't anchor; build understanding incrementally (Grep for entry points, then Read following imports) instead of reading everything upfront; trace usage through wrapper modules by listing exported names, then searching for each.
Choose skills for on-demand, task-specific workflows and CLAUDE.md for always-loaded universal standards.
Enhance MCP tool descriptions so the agent doesn't prefer built-ins like Grep over more capable MCP tools; prefer community MCP servers for standard integrations.

The guide assumes Grep and Glob tools; the docs say they are absent by default on macOS/Linux/WSL, where the same searches run through Bash. The choice (content vs path search) is the same either way.
The repository, the tasks, the read budget and the tool error texts are invented.

examPoints.text: Grep searches file contents for patterns (function names, error messages, imports).
Glob matches file paths by pattern (names, extensions).
Read/Write handle whole files; Edit makes targeted changes by unique text matching.
When Edit fails on non-unique text, fall back to Read + Write.
Choose Grep to search code content across a codebase (all callers of a function, an error message).
Choose Glob to find files matching naming patterns (**/*.test.tsx).
Read the full file, then Write, when Edit can't find a unique anchor.
Build understanding incrementally — Grep for entry points, then Read along imports — instead of reading everything upfront.
Trace usage across wrapper modules: list the exported names first, then search for each.
Choose skills for on-demand, task-specific workflows and CLAUDE.md for always-loaded universal standards.
Describe MCP tools well enough that the agent doesn't prefer built-ins like Grep over a more capable MCP tool.

labIntro:
A small **simulated** repository and five jobs. You call `grep`, `glob`, `read`, `edit` and `write`, shaped like Claude Code's
built-in tools, and `submit()` the answer. The lab checks the answer and counts how many characters you read, as a stand-in for
context. Edit follows the docs' rule: the text must appear **exactly once**, and you must read a file before editing it.

labScenarios.title: Who calls process_refund?
labScenarios.description: Find every file that CALLS process_refund (not the definition, not the docs).

labScenarios.title: Which files are tests?
labScenarios.description: Find every *.test.tsx file, at any depth.

labScenarios.title: One of two identical lines
labScenarios.description: Change the [payments] timeout to 60 - but “timeout = 30” appears in two sections.

labScenarios.title: How is a refund approved?
labScenarios.description: Find the files in the refund-approval flow without blowing the read budget.

labScenarios.title: Callers through a wrapper
labScenarios.description: Which files call the functions the payments wrapper exports (under new names)?

variants.label: ✅ ⭐ Grep for content · Glob for paths · Read + Write fallback · incremental · exported names
variants.code:
import re
from utils.builtin_lab import TASK, EditError, glob, grep, read, submit, write, edit   # SIMULATED repo + tools

if TASK == "find_callers":
    # CONTENT search: which files CALL process_refund? -> Grep (not a file-name search)
    hits = grep(r"process_refund\(")
    submit(sorted({path for path, n, line in hits if not line.lstrip().startswith("def ")}))

elif TASK == "find_tests":
    # PATH pattern: which files are .test.tsx files? -> Glob
    submit(glob("**/*.test.tsx"))

elif TASK == "edit_nonunique":
    # change the PAYMENTS timeout to 60 - "timeout = 30" appears twice
    path = "config/app.toml"
    read(path)
    try:
        edit(path, "timeout = 30", "timeout = 60")
    except EditError:
        # Edit can't anchor uniquely -> Read the whole file, change the right occurrence, Write it back
        text = read(path)
        head, tail = text.split("[payments]")
        write(path, head + "[payments]" + tail.replace("timeout = 30", "timeout = 60", 1))
    submit("done")

elif TASK == "trace_flow":
    # how does a refund get approved? Start at the entry point, then follow the imports - don't read everything
    entry = grep(r"def process_refund\(")[0][0]
    seen, queue = [], [entry]
    while queue:
        path = queue.pop(0)
        if path in seen:
            continue
        seen.append(path)
        for mod in re.findall(r"from (billing\.\w+) import", read(path)):
            queue.append(mod.replace(".", "/") + ".py")
    submit(sorted(seen))

elif TASK == "wrapper_usage":
    # which files call the functions the payments wrapper EXPORTS? First list the exported names...
    names = re.findall(r"'(\w+)'", read("payments/__init__.py").split("__all__")[1])
    # ...then search for each name
    users = {path for name in names for path, n, line in grep(rf"\b{name}\(") if not path.startswith("payments/")}
    submit(sorted(users))
variants.observe: find_callers: Grep 'process_refund\(' → 3 lines; dropping the definition leaves support/bot.py and web/checkout.py. find_tests: Glob '**/*.test.tsx' → the 2 test files. edit_nonunique: Edit fails (“appears 2 times”), so Read + Write changes only [payments]. trace_flow: Grep the entry point, then Read along imports — 3 files, 403 chars. wrapper_usage: Read payments/__init__.py → exports charge_card, issue_refund → Grep each → the 3 shop files.
variants.why: Each job gets the tool built for it, and understanding grows from an entry point instead of from reading everything.

variants.label: ⭐❌ D — Edit fails and nothing else is tried
variants.observe: Edit raised “old_string appears 2 times”; the code swallowed it — the payments timeout is still 30.

questions.q: Before removing the deprecated function legacy_price(), a developer asks the agent to find every place it is called across a 4,000-file repository. A first attempt opened files one by one with Read and, after 25 minutes, had covered about 10% of the code. Which built-in tool fits this step?
opts: Glob for **/*price*, then Read each matching file to look for the calls.
Grep for legacy_price( across the codebase.
Read the files that import pricing modules, one directory at a time.
Bash with a find command listing every file changed in the last year.
questions.explain: Grep searches file contents, which is exactly what finding callers needs. A matches file names, not calls, and misses callers in files named differently. C is the slow file-by-file approach again. D lists files by date, which says nothing about calls.

questions.q: Before a testing-framework migration, the agent must list every React test file. They follow the Component.test.tsx naming and are scattered across 60 folders. The agent's first attempt, a Grep for “describe(”, returned 1,400 matches, including 300 from files that are not tests. Which tool is right?
opts: Grep for “test.tsx” in file contents across the whole repository.
Read the package.json test configuration to find where the test files are.
Glob with **/*.test.tsx.
Grep for “import { render }” to find files that render React components.
questions.explain: Glob matches file paths by pattern, which is what a naming convention needs. A and D search contents for a proxy, which is imprecise. B describes the configuration, not the files.

questions.q: The agent must change timeout = 30 to timeout = 60 only in the [payments] section of a config file. Edit fails because that exact line appears in four sections. On its next attempt the agent edits the first match instead, changing the wrong section. What is the right fallback?
opts: Retry Edit with replace-all enabled, so that every occurrence is changed at once in a single step.
Ask the developer to make the change by hand, since Edit can never target a line that repeats.
Use Grep to count the matches, then Edit whichever one appears closest to the start of the file.
Read the whole file, then Write it back with only the intended section changed.
questions.explain: When Edit can't find unique anchor text, the fallback is Read plus Write, changing only the intended section. A changes all four sections. B gives up on a task the tools can do. C is the “first match” guess that already went wrong.

questions.q: A new engineer asks how an order moves from checkout to fulfilment in an unfamiliar 3,000-file codebase. The agent's first plan is to Read every file under src/ before answering, which would use up most of its context. What is the most effective exploration strategy?
opts: Glob for every file under src/, then Read them in alphabetical order until the flow becomes clear.
Answer from general knowledge of e-commerce systems, then check a few files to confirm the answer.
Grep for the checkout entry point, then Read along the imports it leads to, step by step.
Read the README and the top-level folder names, then describe the whole flow from those alone.
questions.explain: Build understanding incrementally: find the entry point with Grep, then follow imports with Read. A reads everything and fills the context. B starts from assumptions, not the code. D guesses the flow from folder names.

questions.q: A utils/index.ts file re-exports helpers from five internal modules. To find usages of one module, the agent grepped for that module's file name and found 3 matches, although the helpers are used in over 200 files. What should it do instead?
opts: List the names that index.ts exports, then Grep for each of those names across the codebase.
Grep for “utils/index” to find every file that imports the barrel file, and count each as a usage.
Read every file in the repository with “utils” in its path, looking for calls to the helpers.
Conclude that the module is barely used, and report the 3 matches as the complete usage list.
questions.explain: Callers import the re-exported names, not the module's file, so you trace usage by first finding the exported names and then searching for each one. B counts every importer, whether or not it uses this module's helpers. C is slow and too narrow. D reports a false result.

questions.q: A team wants Claude to always use their package manager's commands (pnpm, never npm) in every session. Separately, they have a ten-step release-notes workflow that is needed only on release days, about twice a month. Both currently sit in a 600-line CLAUDE.md. Where should each live?
opts: Both in CLAUDE.md, since everything Claude needs should be loaded at the start of every session.
Both as skills, so neither takes up context until a developer or Claude decides to invoke it.
The release workflow in CLAUDE.md, and the package-manager rule as a skill run before installs.
The package-manager rule in CLAUDE.md, and the release workflow as a skill.
questions.explain: CLAUDE.md is for rules that apply all the time. Skills are for on-demand, task-specific workflows. A loads a twice-a-month workflow into every session. B makes an always-on rule depend on someone invoking it. C gets the two the wrong way round.

questions.q: A team wrote “never edit .env files” in CLAUDE.md, yet in the last month Claude edited a .env file twice while fixing configuration bugs. The team lead now wants a guarantee rather than a better-worded rule. What gives a dependable guarantee in Claude Code?
opts: A permission deny rule, or a PreToolUse hook, that blocks edits to .env files.
The rule moved to the top of CLAUDE.md in capitals, so that the model gives it more weight.
A path-scoped rule in .claude/rules/ that loads the instruction whenever .env files are touched.
A /check-env slash command that developers run after each session to revert any .env changes.
questions.explain: Permission rules and hooks are enforced by Claude Code itself, whatever the model decides. B and C are still instructions, although C loads them at the right moment. D repairs the damage afterwards, if someone remembers.

faq.q: Claude Code on my Mac uses `grep` in Bash, not a Grep tool — is the guide wrong?
faq.a: The docs say the Grep and Glob tools are absent by default on macOS, Linux and WSL, where Claude runs grep and find through Bash. The exam's point is the same either way: content search vs path search.
When every occurrence should change — renaming a variable everywhere in a file, for example. Use a longer anchor, or Read + Write, when only one of several identical lines should change.

faq.q: Isn't reading more files always safer?
faq.a: Not with a finite context. Everything read stays in the conversation. The guide's pattern — Grep for the entry point, Read along imports — keeps the context for what matters.

Built-ins cover most coding tasks. An MCP tool earns its place when it can do something they can't, like search every repository or reach an external system. Its description must say so, or the agent reaches for Grep (TS 2.4 Skill 3).
